parts.label: (a)
parts.text: State what is meant by specific latent heat.

markscheme_points.text: (thermal) energy per unit mass (to change state)
change of state without any change of temperature

hints: Hint 1: Think about what the word specific always means in thermal physics when it appears in front of heat capacity or latent heat.
Hint 2: Think about what happens to the temperature of ice while it is melting at 0 degrees C, even though it is still absorbing energy.
parts.proper_answer: The thermal energy per unit mass required to change state with no change in temperature.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Unpack the word specific**
Think of specific as meaning per unit mass, so per $1\text{ kg}$ or per $1\text{ g}$. You are describing an energy divided by a mass, with unit e.g. $\text{J kg}^{-1}$.

Step 2: **Unpack the words latent heat**
Latent means hidden, because the energy supplied does not show as a temperature rise. It goes into breaking molecular bonds during melting or boiling. So the temperature stays constant while the state changes.

Step 3: **Combine into full definition**
$$L = \frac{Q}{m}$$ where $Q$ is the thermal energy to change state and $m$ is the mass changed, at constant temperature.

parts.label: (b)
parts.part_stem:
A student uses the apparatus illustrated in Fig. 3.1 to determine a value for the specific latent heat of fusion of ice.

{{figure:figure_3_1}}

Fig. 3.1

The balance reading measures the mass of the beaker and the melted ice (water) in the beaker.

The heater is switched on and pieces of ice at $0^{\circ}\text{C}$ are added continuously to the funnel so that the heater is always surrounded by ice.

When water drips out of the funnel at a constant rate, the balance reading is noted at 2.0 minute intervals. After 10 minutes, the current in the heater is increased and the balance readings are taken for a further 12 minutes.

The variation with time of the balance reading is shown in Fig. 3.2.

{{figure:figure_3_2}}

Fig. 3.2

The readings of the ammeter and of the voltmeter are shown in Fig. 3.3.

{{figure:figure_3_3}}

Fig. 3.3

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.text:
From time 0 to time $10.0$ minutes, $65\text{g}$ of ice is melted.

Use Fig. 3.2 to determine the mass of ice melted from time $12.0$ minutes to time $22.0$ minutes.
hints: Hint 1: Read the balance reading from Fig. 3.2 at 12.0 minutes and at 22.0 minutes, then think about how to get just the extra water collected in that interval.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Read the two masses**
From Fig. 3.2, at $t = 12.0\text{ min}$ the reading is about $145\text{ g}$ and at $t = 22.0\text{ min}$ it is about $285\text{ g}$. The beaker mass is included in both, so it will cancel.

Step 2: **Subtract for melted mass**
$$\Delta m = m_{22} - m_{12} \approx 285 - 145 = 140\text{ g}$$ This is the mass of ice melted between 12.0 and 22.0 minutes.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text: Explain why, although the power of the heater is changed, the rate at which thermal energy is transferred from the surroundings to the ice is constant.
hints: Hint 1: Think about what controls how fast heat flows in from the warm room to the cold funnel, and whether the ice temperature ever changes.
parts.proper_answer: The ice remains at $0^{\circ}\text{C}$ and the surroundings remain at constant temperature, so the temperature difference between apparatus and surroundings is constant.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Why surroundings melt ice**
The room is warmer than the ice at $0^{\circ}\text{C}$, so thermal energy flows in by conduction and radiation. The rate of that flow depends on the temperature difference.

Step 2: **Why the rate stays constant**
Fresh ice at $0^{\circ}\text{C}$ is added continuously, so the funnel contents stay at $0^{\circ}\text{C}$. Room temperature is also steady. With a constant temperature difference, the surroundings supply energy at a constant rate, independent of heater power.

parts.label: (b)(iii)
parts.text: Determine a value for the specific latent heat of fusion $L$ of ice.
hints: Hint 1: Think about the two sources of energy that both contribute to melting the ice in each time interval.
Hint 2: Write down the electrical power for each heater setting using the ammeter and voltmeter readings in Fig. 3.3, and convert the 10 minute intervals to seconds.
Hint 3: Think about how you can combine the low-power equation and the high-power equation to cancel out the unknown constant heat from the surroundings.
Hint 4: Use the mass difference of 75 g melted by the extra heater energy alone to find L in J per g.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Energy balance with surroundings**
Let $R$ be the rate of heating from the surroundings in $\text{W}$. In time $t$, heater energy $VIt$ plus surroundings energy $Rt$ melts mass $m$: $$VIt + Rt = mL$$

Step 2: **Write the two experiments**
Low power, $t = 600\text{ s}$, $m = 65\text{ g}$: $$(7.3 \times 1.8 \times 600) + R \times 600 = 65L$$ High power, $t = 600\text{ s}$, $m = 140\text{ g}$: $$(15.1 \times 3.6 \times 600) + R \times 600 = 140L$$

Step 3: **Subtract to eliminate R**
Subtracting removes the identical surroundings term: $$(15.1 \times 3.6 - 7.3 \times 1.8) \times 600 = (140 - 65)L$$ $$(54.36 - 13.14) \times 600 = 75L$$ $$41.22 \times 600 = 75L$$

Step 4: **Calculate L**
$$L = \frac{24732}{75} \approx 330\text{ J g}^{-1}$$ This clever difference method removes the systematic error due to the room.

parts.label: (b)(iv)
parts.text: Calculate the rate at which thermal energy is transferred from the surroundings to the ice.
hints: Hint 1: Think about using your value of L in one of the energy-balance equations, so the only unknown left is the energy supplied by the room.
Hint 2: Remember to divide that total surroundings energy by the 600 s time to get a rate in watts.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Find total surroundings energy**
Use e.g. the low-power run. Total energy needed to melt $65\text{ g}$ is $mL$. Part comes from the heater, the rest $H$ comes from the room: $$VIt + H = mL$$ $$H = mL - VIt = (65 \times 330) - (7.3 \times 1.8 \times 600)$$ $$H \approx 21450 - 7884 \approx 13600\text{ J}$$

Step 2: **Convert to rate**
This $H$ was supplied in $t = 10.0\text{ min} = 600\text{ s}$: $$\text{rate} = \frac{H}{t} = \frac{13600}{600} \approx 23\text{ W}$$
